newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: IBM sees industry-specific network computers.
newsitem.headline: IBM sees industry-specific network computers.

text.p: Low-cost, stripped-down network computers (NCs) are likely to evolve into devices for specific industry uses, Louis Gerstner, Jr, chairman of International Business Machines Corp (IBM) said on Monday.

"Already today we see industry groups starting to create industry network computers. When we think about it, the vast majority of PCs are used in industries to do very specific tasks," he said in reply to a question after a speech.
The NC has limited memory and no peripherals like disk drives. The software that runs on the NCs resides on a network server. IBM introduced its own NC version called Network Station last September.
Gerstner said industry-specific NCs would be a "natural evolution" where network computing would "end the monolithic view of one single device" to meet all needs.
On the debate of whether the NC will spell the death of desktop computers, Gerstner said he saw both co-existing.
"There is no doubt many customers will want full-function PCs but a lot of customers, particularly enterprises, will buy lots of network computers," he said.
He said the NC-PC "fight" was confusing customers who only wanted to do their jobs in the most efficient and effective way.

"The network computer will take hold. There is a big business need for that, but businesses will also need the traditional PC. They will co-exist with a lot of intelligent appliances that will access the network," he said.
Gerstner said he also believed that the NC would reduce the cost of computing.
He said IBM was more interested in helping its customers find solutions to doing their businesses in a competitive way than being sucked into various industry debates.

"The excitement (of network computing) is in the applications. By the year 2000, 75 percent of network investments will be in intranets -- applications within enterprises which will connect enterprises to key business partners," he said.
He said while Internet-based electronic commerce was still exploratory, the potential was enormous.
"Forecasters have estimated US$300 billion in electronic commerce in five years," he said.
Enterprises would have to make "changes in fundamental business processes" to reap the benefits of network computing. He did not spell them out.

Gerstner also made a plea for standards in network computing. "The Internet evolved from one thing and it's not technology. It's agreements on standards that allow computers to talk to any computers," he said.

"The issue is where does choice, control reside -- with customers or with one company. We need customers to stand up and say -- don't deliver things to me that don't comform to industry standards. We won't enjoy the benefits of the networked world without winning this boring but important battle," he said.
